# R0.73G proof: nonlinear relative amplification inside an exact planar barrier

**Date:** 2026-08-30  
**Scope:** the real conjugate pair generated by the R0.73F row

\[
 (K_x,K_z,[K_y]_2)=(0,\pm1,[0]_2)
 \tag{0.1}
\]

around one exact decaying shear with viscosity one  
**Evidence class:** exact perturbation and energy estimates, conditional on
the R0.73F moving-bundle lower bound

## 1. Statement in physical variables

Let

\[
 W(d,x)=-\frac12e^{-d}\sin x+\frac14e^{-4d}\sin2x
 \tag{1.1}
\]

and define on the standard three-torus

\[
 \overline U_\Lambda(t,y)
 =\bigl(0,0,2\Lambda W(4t,2y)\bigr),
 \qquad \Lambda\ge1.
 \tag{1.2}
\]

Because \(W_d=W_{xx}\), equation (1.2) is an exact smooth unforced
Navier--Stokes solution with viscosity one.  Let
\(d_0,K_{\rm F},\alpha,\eta\) denote the constants supplied by R0.73F,
where \(K_{\rm F}\) is its dichotomy prefactor.  For fixed \(D>0\), put

\[
 d_D=\min\{D,d_0\},
 \qquad T_D=\frac{d_D}{4},
 \qquad \kappa_D=(\alpha+\eta)d_D>0.
 \tag{1.3}
\]

**Theorem 1.1.**  There are constants

\[
 C_{\rm top},a,b,C_D,M_D>0,
 \tag{1.4}
\]

independent of \(\Lambda\), and, for every sufficiently large \(\Lambda\),
a real smooth divergence-free unit vector \(\phi_\Lambda\) such that

\[
 \phi_\Lambda\in
 \mathcal S_{2D}:=
 \left\{(0,u_2(y,z),u_3(y,z)):
 \partial_yu_2+\partial_zu_3=0\right\},
 \tag{1.5}
\]

\[
 \|\phi_\Lambda\|_{H^3}\le C_{\rm top}\Lambda^2.
 \tag{1.6}
\]

Define

\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \delta_\Lambda^{\max}:=\min\Bigg\{&
 \frac{a}{4bC_{\rm top}}\Lambda^{-1}e^{-a\Lambda T_D},\\
 &\frac{1}{2K_{\rm F}C_DC_{\rm top}^2}
 \Lambda^{-4}e^{-(M_D-\kappa_D)_+\Lambda}
 \Bigg\}.
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{1.7}
\]

For every \(0<\delta\le\delta_\Lambda^{\max}\), the exact Navier--Stokes
solution with initial datum

\[
 U(0)=\overline U_\Lambda(0)+\delta\phi_\Lambda
 \tag{1.8}
\]

is global and smooth.  Its perturbation
\(w(t)=U(t)-\overline U_\Lambda(t)\) satisfies

\[
 \boxed{
 \|w(T_D)\|_2
 \ge \frac1{2K_{\rm F}}e^{\kappa_D\Lambda}\|w(0)\|_2.}
 \tag{1.9}
\]

It also obeys

\[
 \sup_{0\le t\le T_D}\|w(t)\|_{H^3}
 \le2e^{a\Lambda T_D}\|w(0)\|_{H^3}.
 \tag{1.10}
\]

Equation (1.9) is an exponential **relative** amplification law for a
family of backgrounds and exponentially small seeds.  It is not an
order-one departure theorem.  Every orbit in the theorem stays in the
globally regular planar subsystem (1.5).

## 2. Exact perturbation equation and planar invariance

Write

\[
 U=\overline U_\Lambda+w,
 \qquad \nabla\cdot w=0.
 \tag{2.1}
\]

Subtracting the equation for the background and applying the full
three-dimensional Leray projector gives

\[
 \partial_tw=L_\Lambda(t)w
 -\mathbb P\nabla\cdot(w\otimes w),
 \tag{2.2}
\]

where

\[
 L_\Lambda(t)w
 =\Delta w-\mathbb P\left(
 \overline U_\Lambda\cdot\nabla w
 +w\cdot\nabla\overline U_\Lambda
 \right).
 \tag{2.3}
\]

No Fourier row is removed from the quadratic term in (2.2).

If \(U=(0,U_2(y,z),U_3(y,z))\), then \(U\cdot\nabla\) contains only
\(\partial_y,\partial_z\).  The first component equation has zero initial
datum and zero forcing, while the remaining components solve the periodic
two-dimensional incompressible Navier--Stokes equation in \((y,z)\).
Strong-solution uniqueness therefore preserves \(\mathcal S_{2D}\).
Equivalently, its scalar vorticity

\[
 \omega=\partial_yU_3-\partial_zU_2
 \tag{2.4}
\]

satisfies

\[
 \partial_t\omega+U_2\partial_y\omega+U_3\partial_z\omega
 =\Delta_{y,z}\omega
 \tag{2.5}
\]

and hence

\[
 \frac12\frac d{dt}\|\omega\|_2^2
 +\|\nabla_{y,z}\omega\|_2^2=0.
 \tag{2.6}
\]

Standard two-dimensional regularity gives global smoothness for smooth
data.  Thus the nonlinear continuation used below cannot produce
three-dimensional vortex stretching or a singularity.

## 3. A smooth launch with polynomial Sobolev cost

Let \(x=2y\) be the normalized shear coordinate and

\[
 L=-\partial_x^2+\frac14,
 \qquad \varepsilon=\Lambda^{-1}.
 \tag{3.1}
\]

At profile time \(d=0\), the R0.73F kinetic generator is

\[
 \widetilde B_\varepsilon(0)
 =\widetilde A(0)-\varepsilon L.
 \tag{3.2}
\]

Choose an \(L^2_x\)-normalized eigenvector \(h_\varepsilon\) in its
nonzero finite-dimensional top spectral subspace:

\[
 \widetilde B_\varepsilon(0)h_\varepsilon
 =\lambda_\varepsilon h_\varepsilon,
 \qquad \|h_\varepsilon\|_2=1.
 \tag{3.3}
\]

The common R0.73F contour bounds \(|\lambda_\varepsilon|\), while the
explicit finite-harmonic operator \(\widetilde A(0)\) is bounded on every
fixed \(H^m_x\).  Ellipticity and the eigenvalue equation therefore give,
first for \(m=0\) and then for \(m=2\),

\[
 \|h_\varepsilon\|_{H^{m+2}_x}
 \le C_m\varepsilon^{-1}\|h_\varepsilon\|_{H^m_x},
 \tag{3.4}
\]

so

\[
 \|h_\varepsilon\|_{H^4_x}
 \le C\varepsilon^{-2}=C\Lambda^2.
 \tag{3.5}
\]

The exact kinetic-to-velocity map on the physical \(K_z=1\) row is

\[
 \mathcal Eh(y,z)=
 \left(
 0,\frac12(L^{-1/2}h)(2y),
 i(\partial_xL^{-1/2}h)(2y)
 \right)e^{iz}.
 \tag{3.6}
\]

It is divergence free and isometric in the normalized kinetic and physical
velocity \(L^2\) norms.  The map is order zero in every fixed Sobolev
scale.  Hence the real conjugate-pair launch

\[
 \phi_\Lambda=2^{-1/2}
 \left(\mathcal Eh_\varepsilon+
 \overline{\mathcal Eh_\varepsilon}\right)
 \tag{3.7}
\]

has \(\|\phi_\Lambda\|_2=1\), belongs to \(\mathcal S_{2D}\), and obeys
(1.6).

R0.73F proves its moving-bundle inverse estimate for every vector in the
frozen top space.  The positive and negative physical rows are conjugate
and orthogonal.  Converting profile time \(d=4t\) to physical time therefore
gives

\[
 \|\mathcal U_\Lambda(T_D,0)\phi_\Lambda\|_2
 \ge K_{\rm F}^{-1}e^{\kappa_D\Lambda}.
 \tag{3.8}
\]

This is the only input from the R0.73F lower theorem.

## 4. Fixed-window \(H^3\) bootstrap

Let

\[
 Y(t)=\|w(t)\|_{H^3}.
 \tag{4.1}
\]

The finite-harmonic background satisfies

\[
 \sup_{0\le t\le T_D}
 \|\overline U_\Lambda(t)\|_{W^{4,\infty}}
 \le C\Lambda.
 \tag{4.2}
\]

Apply derivatives of order at most three to (2.2).  The leading background
transport term cancels by incompressibility.  The remaining background
commutators and \(w\cdot\nabla\overline U_\Lambda\) contribute at most
\(C\Lambda Y^2\).  Since
\(H^3(\mathbb T^3)\hookrightarrow W^{1,\infty}\), the standard transport
estimate for the quadratic term is at most \(CY^3\).  Thus

\[
 \frac12\frac d{dt}Y^2+\|\nabla w\|_{H^3}^2
 \le A\Lambda Y^2+BY^3.
 \tag{4.3}
\]

After increasing constants,

\[
 Y'\le a\Lambda Y+bY^2.
 \tag{4.4}
\]

Scalar comparison gives

\[
 Y(t)\le
 \frac{a\Lambda Y(0)e^{a\Lambda t}}
 {a\Lambda-bY(0)(e^{a\Lambda t}-1)}.
 \tag{4.5}
\]

If

\[
 Y(0)\le\rho_\Lambda
 :=\frac{a\Lambda}{4b}e^{-a\Lambda T_D},
 \tag{4.6}
\]

the denominator in (4.5) is at least \(3a\Lambda/4\), and therefore

\[
 Y(t)\le\frac43e^{a\Lambda t}Y(0)
 <2e^{a\Lambda t}Y(0),
 \qquad0\le t\le T_D.
 \tag{4.7}
\]

Global existence follows independently from planar invariance; (4.7) is
the quantitative estimate needed for nonlinear shadowing.

## 5. All-mode quadratic remainder

Let

\[
 z_t=L_\Lambda(t)z,
 \qquad z(0)=w(0),
 \tag{5.1}
\]

and set \(r=w-z\).  Then

\[
 r_t=L_\Lambda(t)r
 -\mathbb P\nabla\cdot(w\otimes w),
 \qquad r(0)=0.
 \tag{5.2}
\]

The background transport cancels in the \(L^2\) energy identity, while

\[
 \left|\langle r\cdot\nabla\overline U_\Lambda,r\rangle\right|
 \le C\Lambda\|r\|_2^2.
 \tag{5.3}
\]

For the complete quadratic forcing, without a row projection,

\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \left|\langle\mathbb P\nabla\cdot(w\otimes w),r\rangle\right|
 &=\left|\langle w\otimes w,\nabla r\rangle\right|\\
 &\le C\|w\|_\infty\|w\|_2\|\nabla r\|_2\\
 &\le\frac12\|\nabla r\|_2^2+CY^4.
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{5.4}
\]

Consequently,

\[
 \frac d{dt}\|r\|_2^2
 \le c\Lambda\|r\|_2^2+CY^4.
 \tag{5.5}
\]

Using \(r(0)=0\) and (4.7),

\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \|r(T_D)\|_2^2
 &\le C\int_0^{T_D}
 e^{c\Lambda(T_D-s)}Y(s)^4\,ds\\
 &\le16CT_D
 e^{(c+4a)\Lambda T_D}Y(0)^4.
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{5.6}
\]

Thus, with

\[
 C_D=4(CT_D)^{1/2},
 \qquad M_D=\left(\frac c2+2a\right)T_D,
 \tag{5.7}
\]

one has

\[
 \boxed{
 \|r(T_D)\|_2
 \le C_De^{M_D\Lambda}\|w(0)\|_{H^3}^2.}
 \tag{5.8}
\]

This estimate includes every Fourier mode generated by convolution.

## 6. Closing the nonlinear lower bound

Take \(w(0)=\delta\phi_\Lambda\).  Equations (1.6) and the first term in
(1.7) imply \(Y(0)\le\rho_\Lambda\), so (4.7) and (5.8) apply.  The second
term in (1.7) gives

\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \|r(T_D)\|_2
 &\le C_De^{M_D\Lambda}
 C_{\rm top}^2\Lambda^4\delta^2\\
 &\le\frac1{2K_{\rm F}}e^{\kappa_D\Lambda}\delta.
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{6.1}
\]

By (3.8) and the reverse triangle inequality,

\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \|w(T_D)\|_2
 &\ge\|z(T_D)\|_2-\|r(T_D)\|_2\\
 &\ge\frac1{2K_{\rm F}}e^{\kappa_D\Lambda}\delta.
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{6.2}
\]

This proves (1.9).  The sufficient ceiling (1.7) can decay faster than
\(e^{-\kappa_D\Lambda}\).  The theorem therefore does not show that
\(\|w(T_D)\|_2\) stays bounded below by a positive constant.  It only
retains at least half of the certified linear gain ratio on a smaller seed
scale.

## 7. Exact leakage from the selected row

Write the positive physical row using the normalized shear coordinate
\(x=2y\):

\[
 u_v(y,z)=\left(0,v(2y),2iv'(2y)\right)e^{iz}.
 \tag{7.1}
\]

It is divergence free.  Direct multiplication gives

\[
 (u_v\cdot\nabla)u_v
 =\left(0,0,4i\bigl(vv''-(v')^2\bigr)(2y)\right)e^{2iz}.
 \tag{7.2}
\]

The Leray projection of a field
\((0,0,g(2y))e^{2iz}\) vanishes exactly when \(g\) is constant.  If

\[
 vv''-(v')^2=\text{constant},
 \tag{7.3}
\]

then differentiation gives \(vv'''-v'v''=0\).  On intervals where
\(v\ne0\), the quotient \(v''/v\) is constant.  Analytic continuation and
periodicity yield

\[
 v(x)=Ae^{inx}+Be^{-inx}
 \tag{7.4}
\]

for an integer \(n\ge0\), including the constant case at \(n=0\).

No nonzero frozen viscous top eigenvector has the form (7.4).  Indeed, its
wall-normal profile satisfies the normalized frozen equation

\[
 \sigma Lv
 =-\frac i2\bigl(WLv+W_{xx}v\bigr)-\varepsilon L^2v.
 \tag{7.5}
\]

At \(d=0\), the coefficient \(W_2\) of \(e^{2ix}\) is nonzero.  If the
coefficient \(A\) in (7.4) is nonzero, the \((n+2)\)-Fourier coefficient
inside the bracket \(WLv+W_{xx}v\) in (7.5) is

\[
 W_2\left(n^2+\frac14-4\right)A
 =W_2\left(n^2-\frac{15}{4}\right)A\ne0.
 \tag{7.6}
\]

The left side and the viscous term have no such coefficient.  If \(A=0\),
the symmetric coefficient generated from \(B\) gives the same
contradiction; \(n=0\) is covered by the generated \(\pm2\) coefficients.
Thus the projected double-row forcing in (7.2) is nonzero for the selected
top vector.

For the real seed \(u_v+\overline{u_v}\), the first quadratic convolution
has physical \(K_z\)-channels \(0,+2,-2\); none is the original
\(+1\) or \(-1\) channel.  Feedback into the original pair therefore begins
no earlier than the next interaction, which is cubic in the seed amplitude.
The single row is not a nonlinear invariant subsystem, although the full
planar space \(\mathcal S_{2D}\) is invariant.

## 8. Exact boundary

The following statements are closed for the selected family:

- the physical perturbation equation and planar invariant class;
- a polynomial \(H^3\) cost for one frozen top eigenvector;
- a fixed-window \(H^3\) bootstrap with an explicit sufficient seed ceiling;
- an all-mode quadratic remainder estimate;
- nonlinear relative amplification by at least
  \((2K_{\rm F})^{-1}e^{\kappa_D\Lambda}\);
- nonzero leakage from the selected row into the double row;
- global smoothness of every nonlinear orbit constructed here.

The following remain open:

- a natural seed of size \(e^{-\kappa_D\Lambda}\) that reaches order one;
- a harmonic-resolved bilinear estimate with the sharp unstable exponent;
- a genuinely transverse \(K_x\ne0\) or first-velocity-component launch;
- a repeated three-dimensional triad cascade;
- any singularity or global-regularity conclusion for general 3D data.

The R0.73F row is therefore a rigorous nonlinear transient-growth
mechanism, but its direct nonlinear continuation is an exact globally
regular two-dimensional route.
